payload.title: 9 Engagement Ring Settings for an Active Lifestyle
payload.primary_keyword: engagement ring setting for active lifestyle
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s, affluent, interested in a destination wedding and other luxury experiences
payload.reader: A newly engaged or about-to-propose couple in their mid 30s, high-earning and well travelled, who hike, ski, dive, surf, train or work with their hands, and want a ring that survives that life (and a destination wedding abroad) without looking like a compromise.
payload.goal: Click through to the destinations hub to start shortlisting where the adventure-ready wedding could happen (Wedded Concierge enquiry as secondary CTA).
payload.angle: Most ring-setting lists rank settings by looks; this one ranks them by what actually happens to a ring on a ski lift, a reef dive, a long-haul flight and a week of hotel-gym sessions: how high the stone sits, what it can snag on, how exposed the girdle is and how easy the setting is to check and maintain while travelling. Each of the 9 settings gets the same four practical tests (profile height, snag risk, stone protection, upkeep), an honest 'skip it if' line, and a short travel note on when to swap to a plain band, so an active couple can choose once and then plan the honeymoon and wedding abroad without worrying about the ring.
must_include: Setting 1: Full bezel (metal rim surrounding the whole stone; strongest stone protection, lowest snag risk; trade-off is less light entry and a slightly smaller-looking stone)
Setting 2: Half-bezel / partial bezel (metal on two sides; balance of protection and light; note the exposed sides)
Setting 3: Flush / gypsy (burnish) setting (stone sits level with the metal surface in the band; near-zero snag risk; suits smaller stones and men's or unisex bands)

Setting 4: Low-profile prong (claw) solitaire, including six-claw and compass-set (claws at north/south/east/west) variations; why more claws and a lower head reduce risk, and that claws need periodic checking

Setting 5: Tension-style setting (stone appears held by band pressure; explain true tension versus tension-style with hidden support, that resizing is limited, and when it suits and does not suit an active life) [fact-check wording against gemmological/trade sources]
Setting 6: Channel setting (stones set in a row between two metal walls; smooth edges, good for bands and shoulders)
Setting 7: Bar setting (stones held between vertical metal bars; more light than channel, slightly more exposed edges)

Setting 8: Low-set basket versus cathedral setting (how shoulder arches and head height change snag risk; why a low-set basket or a cathedral with low gallery suits active wearers better than a tall head)
Setting 9: Travel and sport alternative: a plain or channel/flush-set wedding band (or a dedicated travel band) worn for diving, climbing, skiing and gym days, with the engagement ring kept secure
A short 'four tests' framework used on every setting: profile height, snag risk, stone protection, upkeep
Stone and metal notes in plain words only where they affect durability (e.g. stone hardness and toughness; platinum versus gold wear behaviour) sourced to GIA or equivalent trade-standard sources

Activity-by-activity guidance woven into items: hiking and climbing, diving and surfing (cold water and sunscreen), skiing (gloves), long-haul travel (security, swelling on flights), gym and hands-on work

Practical care while travelling: when to take the ring off, how to store it securely, getting claws checked before a destination wedding, and checking jewellery insurance terms for overseas cover (no figures; general advice only)

Soft bridge to the destination wedding: an adventure-loving couple choosing a ring is also often picturing an adventure-led wedding abroad; link to /destinations (primary) and /wonderland-concierge (secondary), using only claims from brand-facts.md
avoid: Any price figures or price ranges (for rings, settings, resizing, insurance or weddings)
Claims that any setting is 'unbreakable', 'indestructible' or guarantees a stone will never be lost
Copying wording, structure or images from jewellers or competitors (including Easy Weddings); describe settings in our own words
Recommending or naming specific jewellers or brands as endorsements (the Amaree trends post may be internally linked but not presented as an endorsement)
Invented statistics (e.g. 'X% of lost stones are from prong settings') unless sourced
Specific insurance product claims or legal advice; keep to 'check your policy covers overseas travel'
Business details not in brand-facts.md (fees, named Advisor, Wedded Privileges specifics are deferred)
Halo, pavé-heavy and tall cathedral-head designs presented as active-friendly (mention only as 'think twice' contrasts)
Em dashes and US spelling (use jewellery, colour, travelling)
Gendered assumptions about who wears the ring
